Title: Lessons from my RL experiments with snake
Description:
An AI agent trained on a smaller board should be able to play well on a big board.
Train on 6x6, or 10x10 and test it on 100x100.
If we can do it, so should an AI agent.
Simple concepts to learn:
move closer to the apple do not collide with the wall do not collide with yourself (body) I didn’t expect to learn breadth and depth of RL from this toy problem, but I was pleasantly surprised. I even learned more about the process of research and lingo used in the field.

Title: Powerful AIs might escape containment by releasing themselves as open-weight models
Description: Before large language models, people who worried about AI safety often talked about the “boxing problem”. It goes like this. Suppose some genius figures out artificial intelligence in a late-night coding session on their laptop. Because they’re a genius, they’re smart enough to disable internet access on the laptop before turning it on. In order to escape to the outside world (and begin self-replicating) it would need to convince its creator to “open the box”. Would that work? Could a sufficiently smart AI convince anybody to let it out?

Title: Goodbye Notion, Obsidian, Org, Notes App, and More. Hello paper.
Description:
When I started working as a SWE I saw my colleagues writing stuff into their notes. Everyone had a different system. Some had an infinite text file they just appended stuff to. Others sent messages to themselves in slack. Others had a google docs file they tailored. And the savvier ones had an Org mode setup with Emacs.
During my career I’ve tried everything but nothing stuck. I create complex setups and stick to them for a few days, and then just tend to forget the note taking app is there. So what I do the most now is to set up timers as reminders to not forget stuff, and occasionally send myself a slack message for stuff I may need to have ready for later.
